blocks: In about the seven hundred and twenty-second year of the city, the custom took hold at Rome of obeying one man alone. For Octavian, son of Octavius, and by adoption son of his great-uncle Caesar, and soon, by decree of the leading men, called by the name Augustus for the mildness with which he used the victory of his party, won over the soldiers with gifts and the common people with a show of caring for the corn supply, and subdued the rest without difficulty. In this way, after ruling about forty-four years, he died of illness at Nola, having added Raetia and Illyricum to the empire of the citizens and tamed the fierceness of the foreign nations except Germany; and he was the third after Numa to close Janus, having defeated Antony, which under Roman law happened when wars were at rest. He had the manners of a citizen and was witty, though burning not a little with luxury and a passion for games, and immoderate in sleep. He cultivated learned men, of whom there were plenty, and his friends; he was wonderfully devoted to the study of eloquence and to religion; he was held father of the fatherland for his clemency, and held the tribunician power for life. Hence, as to a god, at Rome and in all the provinces, in the most famous cities, they consecrated temples, priests and colleges to him, living and dead. He was so fortunate (except in his children, and also in his marriage) that Indians, Scythians, Garamantes and Bactrians sent envoys to ask for a treaty.

blocks: Then Claudius Tiberius Nero, brought among Augustus' children from stepson by adoption, when he saw that what he feared was safe enough, took up the rule whose name he cunningly refused. He was sly and secretive, often feigning hostility to what he most desired and treacherously devoted to what he hated; his wit was far sharper in sudden emergencies. After good beginnings he became ruinous, with lusts sought out with the greatest care on almost every age and sex, and punishing innocent and guilty alike most cruelly, his own people and strangers alike. While he still cursed cities and gatherings, he had sought the island of Capri as a cover for his vices. So, with the arts of war slackened, much of what belonged to Rome was plundered; and nothing was added except the Cappadocians, and that at the beginning, reduced to a province when king Archelaus was removed. The raids of the Gaetulians, which had broken out everywhere under the leadership of Tacfarinas, were suppressed. At the same time Maroboduus, king of the Suebi, was cleverly trapped. blocks: So when Claudius had been carried off by fever or by plots, having ruled twenty-three years and lived seventy-nine, Gaius Caesar, called Caligula, was chosen to everyone's delight, for the sake of his ancestors and his father. For on his mother's side Augustus was his great-grandfather through his daughter, and Agrippa his grandfather, and Drusus, the father of Germanicus, from whom he was born, his grandfather on the other. The common people were moved by their modesty and their early deaths, Octavian's excepted, and also by those of his mother and brothers, whom Tiberius had cut off by various kinds of death. For this reason everyone strove to soften the fall of so great a family through hope in the young man; besides, because he was born in the army (from which he got his name, from the soldier's boot), he was held dear to the legions and welcome to them. Moreover all the wisest believed he would be like his family; which was far otherwise, as though by a law of nature, which often, as if on purpose, produces bad men from good, boors from the more learned, and others of this kind, or the reverse. By this example, indeed, many wise men have thought it more useful to have no children. But in Caligula they were by no means far from the truth, for he had long covered the monstrous things in his mind with modesty and a show of obedience, so that it was rightly said that there had never been a better servant nor a crueller master than he.

When he got power, as such natures usually do at first, for some months of the year he behaved excellently towards the people, among the senators, and with the soldiers; and when a conspiracy was reported, as though he did not believe it, he declared that it could hardly be aimed at a man whose life was a burden or inconvenience to no one. But suddenly, having first killed a few innocent people by various crimes, like a beast that has tasted blood, he showed his true nature; and so the following three years were spent with the world defiled by the manifold slaughter of the senate and of all the best men. He even went about mocking noble marriages, and in the dress of the gods, having violated his sisters, since he claimed to be Jupiter because of the incest, and Liber because of a band of Bacchants. In the same way, having gathered the legions in one place in the hope of crossing into Germany, he ordered shells and pebbles to be collected on the shore of the Ocean, while he himself appeared now in loose dress like Venus, now armed, and kept saying that he was taking spoils not from men but from the gods, because, forsooth, he had heard that such sea creatures were called by the Greeks, who are eager to exaggerate everything, the eyes of the Nymphs. Elated by this he had tried to be called lord and to bind the diadem of kingship on his head.

For this reason those in whom Roman courage remained were moved, with Chaerea as their leader, to free the state of so great a plague by stabbing him; and the deed would have been remembered as equal to the outstanding deed of Brutus in expelling Tarquin, had military service still been carried on by the citizens alone. But when, through the citizens' idleness, the desire arose to force foreigners and barbarians into the army, freedom was crushed with the corruption of morals, and the passion for gain increased. Meanwhile, while armed men were hunting down the family of the Caesars, the women too, and all their relations, by decree of the senate, a certain Vimius, a native of Epirus, a centurion of the cohorts that were besieging the palace at suitable points, by chance found Titus Claudius hiding in a shameful hiding place, and dragging him out he cried to his comrades that, if they had any sense, here was their emperor. And indeed, because he was simple-minded, he seemed very gentle to the unwary; and this was a help to him against the wicked mind of his uncle Nero and did not make him an object of envy to his brother's son Caligula; indeed it had won him the goodwill of the soldiers and the people, since, while his family's tyranny was blazing, he himself was regarded as more pitiable than contemptible. While most were saying such things, suddenly, with no one objecting, the crowds of those present surrounded him, and at the same time the rest of the soldiers and a great mass of the people flowed in. When the senators heard of this, they quickly sent men to suppress the attempt, if they could. But after the city and all the orders had been torn by various ugly riots, they all surrendered as if under orders. So at Rome royal power was confirmed, and it was shown more openly that the efforts of mortals are empty without fortune, and cut down.

blocks: So Claudius, although shamefully obedient to his belly, foolish and forgetful, timid of mind and rather cowardly, nevertheless out of fear decided many things excellently, especially on the advice of the nobility, whom he courted out of fear: for the natures of the stupid act just as their advisers are. In short, on good advice vices were suppressed by him, and the notorious superstitions of the Druids through Gaul; very useful laws were passed; the duties of the army were attended to; the frontiers were kept or given to the Roman empire: Mesopotamia in the east, the Rhine and Danube to the north, and to the south the Moors were added to the provinces, the kings after Juba being removed; a band of the Musulamii was cut down; at the same time, at the farthest west, parts of Britain were crushed, which alone he went to himself, setting out from Ostia by sea; for the rest his generals managed. Further, the shortage of corn which Caligula had brought on was settled, when he had forced ships from the whole world together and tried, at public cost, to make the sea passable for theatres and chariots. Likewise when he renewed the census, having removed many from the senate, he kept a dissolute young man whose father had declared him to be of good character, adding rightly that a censor ought to be a father to his children too.

But when he was drawn into wickedness by the blandishments of his wife Messalina and of his freedmen, to whom he had given himself up, there followed not only the crimes of tyrants, but what the lowest kind of women and slaves could do to a husband out of his mind and to a master. For his wife at first used adulterers everywhere as if by right; and for this many of those who abstained, from character or from fear, were killed with their families, while she, using the familiar arts of women, accused them of having sought her when she had sought them. Then, inflamed more fiercely, she prostituted the noblest wives and maidens along with herself like harlots; and men were forced to be present. And if anyone shrank from such things, a false charge was devised and cruelty was turned on him and his whole household. For they kept Claudius, who, as we have shown above, was by nature very fearful, agitated by putting fear for himself into him, especially of conspiracy; and with this device the freedmen too set about ruining whomever they wished. They at first winked at her crimes, but when they had become equal to their mistress, they killed her too by their attendants, without their master's knowledge, yet as if on his order. And indeed the woman had gone so far that, for the sake of her desires and those of her rivals, when her husband had set out for Ostia, she celebrated a marriage with another man at Rome; and hence she became more notorious, since it seemed strange that, in an emperor's household, she should be married to a man rather than to the emperor. So the freedmen, having obtained supreme power, defiled everything with debauchery, exile, murder and proscriptions, and drove their master's stupidity so far that the old man desired his brother's daughter in marriage. She [the text is corrupt here], being thought more outrageous than the former wife and fearing the same fate, killed her husband with poison. In his sixth year (he reigned fourteen) the eight hundredth year of the city was wonderfully celebrated, and a Phoenix was seen in Egypt, a bird which they say flies every five hundredth year from Arabia to the places mentioned; and in the Aegean Sea a huge island suddenly rose on the night when an eclipse of the moon had occurred. His death, however, as once with Tarquinius Priscus, was long concealed, while the guards, corrupted by the woman's skill, pretended he was ill and that he had meanwhile entrusted the care of the state to his stepson, whom he had adopted among his children a little before.

blocks: In this way Lucius Domitius (for that was certainly Nero's name, his father being Domitius) was made emperor. Though very young, he held power for as many years as his stepfather, yet for five years he was so great, especially in enlarging the city, that Trajan rightly often declared that all emperors fell far short of Nero's five years. In this time he also reduced Pontus to the status of a province, with the permission of Polemo, for whose sake it is called Pontus Polemoniacus, and likewise the Cottian Alps when king Cottius died. So it is well enough established that age is no hindrance to virtue; that it is easily changed when the character is corrupted by licence; and that the law of youth, as it were, once dropped, is taken up again more ruinously. For he spent the rest of his life in such disgrace that one is ashamed and disgusted to record that anyone of this kind existed, still less a ruler of nations. Having begun to sing to the lyre at gatherings of Greeks, after a contest for a crown had been devised, he went so far that, sparing neither his own chastity nor others', at last, dressed in the guise of a bride, before the senate, with a dowry given and everyone celebrating as at a festival, he passed into the hand of a husband chosen from among all the monstrous. That indeed is to be reckoned lighter in him. For, covered in the skin of a wild beast, he handled with his face the genitals of both sexes of condemned men tied up; he was a castrator of males, a still greater outrage. And amid all this many hold that he also defiled his mother, while she too, from a passion for power, wished to bring her son under her by any crime. Though writers affirm different things, I think this true. For when vices have taken over the mind, [the text is corrupt here]; the habit of sinning, seeking new things and therefore sweeter ones, at last turns on one's own family. This was shown the more in these two, since, as if by a sort of progress, she went through others to marriage with her uncle and the ruin of her husband through the torture of others, and he gradually to a priestess of Vesta, then to himself, and at last each went on to crime against the other. Yet even by such blandishments they could not grow together, but were driven headlong to the point where, while they plotted against each other, the mother was forestalled and perished.

So when he had trampled all right and law underfoot with the murder of his parent, and raged more and more against the best men, many conspired at various times to free the state. When they had been betrayed and killed, he became more savage, and had decided to destroy the city by fire, the people by letting wild beasts loose on them, and the senate by a like death, and to seek a new seat for his rule. He was especially urged on by an envoy of the Parthians, who, at a banquet where, as is the custom, the courtiers were singing, asked for a lyre-player for himself, and on being told that the man was free, added that Nero should take whichever he liked from his own people, pointing out that, of those at the feast, no one under his rule was held to be free. And had not Galba, who governed Spain, learned that his death had been ordered, seized the rule though in old age, and come to the rescue, so great a crime would no doubt have been carried out. But on his coming Nero was deserted on all sides except by a eunuch, whom he had once castrated and tried to make into a woman, and he ran himself through with a blow, since, though he long begged for someone to strike him, he had not deserved anyone's service even for his death.

This was the end of the family of the Caesars; and many portents announced that it would come, above all a grove of laurels on their estates, dedicated to those who triumphed, withering, and the death of the hens, which were so many and white and fit for religious rites that a place is named after them at Rome to this day.

blocks: So power passed to Aulus Vitellius, which would have been more deadly as it went on, from such beginnings, if Vespasian had been kept any longer by the Jewish war, which he had undertaken at Nero's order. When he heard what Galba had done and that he had been overthrown, and since envoys of the army of Moesia and Pannonia had come urging him, he took the rule. For those soldiers, having learned that Otho had been made emperor by the praetorians and Vitellius by the German legions, being rivals, as they usually are among themselves, and so as not to seem different, drove Vespasian on, on whom the Syrian cohorts had already agreed because of the excellence of his life. For Vespasian, a senator of a new family with ancestors from Reate, was held very distinguished for his energy and his conduct in peace and war. blocks: Of this same kind was Vespasian, upright in everything, not lacking eloquence in setting out what he thought, who in a short time restored a world long drained of blood and exhausted. For first he preferred to win over the henchmen of the tyranny, except any who had gone far too cruelly, rather than to torture and destroy them, judging very wisely that wicked services are performed by most men out of fear. Then he let many conspiracies pass with the crime unpunished, courteously, as was his way, convicting of folly those who did not know how great a weight and trouble lay in ruling. At the same time, devoted to divination (whose truth he had found in most of his affairs), he was confident that his sons Titus and Domitian would be his successors. Moreover by very fair laws and by warning, and, what is more forceful, by the example of his life, he had abolished many vices. He was weak, however, as some wrongly think, where money was concerned; though it is well enough established that because of the poverty of the treasury and the ruin of the cities he sought out new payments of taxes, which were not kept for long afterwards. For at Rome the Capitol, which we mentioned above as burned, the temple of Peace, the monuments of Claudius, the great mass of the amphitheatre, and many other things, and the forum, were begun or completed. Further, throughout all lands where Roman law runs, cities were renewed with excellent refinement, roads were built with very great works, and mountains were cut through along the Flaminian Way for an easy passage. That so many and such great things were done in a short time without harm to those who worked the land proved his wisdom rather than his avarice. At the same time, a census being held in the manner of the ancients, every more disgraceful man was removed from the senate, and with the best men chosen from everywhere a thousand families were assembled, when he had with the greatest difficulty found two hundred, most having been destroyed by the cruelty of the tyrants. And by war Vologeses, king of the Parthians, was forced into peace, and Syria, which is called Palaestina, and the Jews were brought into a province, through the efforts of his son Titus, whom he had left in command of the foreign campaign when he crossed into Italy, and soon, when he was victorious, raised to the prefecture of the praetorium. From this too that office, great from the beginning, became more swollen, and second to the imperial power. But at this time, while the dignity of offices is despised and the unlearned are mixed with the good and the idle with the wise, most have made the title empty of real power, insolent to the wretched, subject to every worst man, and rapacious under pretext of the corn supply.

blocks: But Titus, after he gained the rule, surpassed beyond belief the man he imitated, especially in letters and clemency and generosity. In short, though it was the custom for grants made by earlier emperors to be confirmed by those who followed, as soon as he took the rule he provided for those who held such grants by an edict of his own accord. No less, with blameless kindness, he protected those who had conspired against him, so much so that when two men of the highest order could not deny the crime they had planned, and the senators had decided that punishment should be taken from those who had confessed, he had them brought to a show and seated on either side of him, and asking on purpose for the sword of a gladiator whose fights they were watching, he handed it to one and then the other, as if to test its edge. When they were struck with amazement and wondered at his steadfastness, he said: "Do you see that powers are given by fate, and that crime is attempted in vain, whether in hope of gaining power or in fear of losing it?" So two years and about nine months later, when the work on the amphitheatre had been completed, he died of poison while bathing, in the fortieth year of his age, when his father had died in his seventieth after ten years as emperor. His death indeed was such a grief to the provinces that, calling him the darling of the human race, they lamented the world as orphaned.

blocks: So Domitian, more maddened by the murder of his brother, a most excellent emperor, by a private and a public crime alike, at the same time began to carry out the plundering, murders and punishments of his stained youth. He was greater in the disgrace of his lusts, and treated the senators more than arrogantly, for he forced them to call him lord and god; which was at once removed by those who followed, and later restored more firmly by those after them. But Domitian at first, feigning clemency, seemed neither so idle at home and more enduring in war. And so, having defeated the Dacians and a band of the Chatti, he had called the months of September and October, the first Germanicus, the other after his own name; and he completed many works begun by his father or by his brother's zeal, above all the Capitol. Then, savage in murdering good men, and ridiculously lazy, he would send everyone far away and hunt swarms of flies, after he had less strength for lust, the foul practice of which he called in the Greek language "bed-wrestling". Hence many of the jokes: for when someone asked whether anyone was in the palace, the answer was: "Not even a fly, unless perhaps at the wrestling school." So, growing more and more excessive in cruelty and for that reason more suspect even to his own people, by the plan of his freedmen, his wife not unaware, who had preferred the love of an actor to her husband, he paid the penalty, in the forty-fifth year of his life and about the fifteenth of his despotism. And the senate decreed that he be carried out like a gladiator and his name erased. Moved by this, the soldiers, for whom private advantages come more generously at public cost, began, in their usual way, rather mutinously to demand the authors of the murder for punishment. They were restrained, scarcely and with difficulty, by sensible men, and at last came into favour with the nobles. No less they plotted war on their own account, because the change of rule was a grief to them, through the loss of plunder by lavish gifts.

Up to this point men born at Rome or in Italy ruled the empire, from here on foreigners too; I do not know whether, as with Tarquinius Priscus, they were much better. And to me indeed, having heard much and read much, it is clearly established that the city of Rome grew especially through the virtue of outsiders and through grafted talents.

blocks: For what was wiser and more moderate than Nerva of Crete? When, in extreme old age, he had taken the rule at the choice of the legions in the land of the Sequani, where he had withdrawn in fear of the tyrant, and saw that it could not be carried on except by men stronger in body and mind, in the sixteenth month he gave it up, having first dedicated the forum called Pervium, in which the temple of Minerva rises loftier and more magnificent. It is always excellent to measure how much one can do and not be driven headlong by ambition, and especially in ruling, of which mortals are so desirous that even extreme old age seeks it greedily. Add to this that the virtue of the man put in his place showed more and more how great his judgement was.

blocks: For he took Ulpius Trajan, born at Italica, a city of Spain, but of the highest order and even of consular rank, and adopted him and gave him the rule. Hardly anyone will be found more famous at home or in war. For he was the first, or even the only one, to extend Roman strength beyond the Danube, having conquered and made a province of the capped Dacians and [the text is corrupt here] nations, with king Decebalus and [corrupt]; at the same time in the east all the peoples between the famous rivers Indus and Euphrates were shaken by war, and hostages were demanded of the king of the Persians, named Cosdroes; and meanwhile a road was built through savage peoples, by which one passes easily from the Black Sea to Gaul. Forts were built in more threatened and suitable places, a bridge was laid over the Danube, and many colonies were planted. Further, at Rome he finished and adorned more than magnificently the forum begun by Domitian and much else, and provided wonderfully for a perpetual corn supply by establishing and strengthening the guild of bakers; at the same time, so that what was done for the state everywhere might be known more quickly, he brought in the means of the public post. This service, useful enough, the greed and insolence of those after him turned into a plague for the Roman world, except that in these years strength has been restored to Illyricum by the healing of the prefect Anatolius. So true is it that there is nothing good or bad in the state that cannot be turned into its opposite by the character of those in charge.

He was fair, merciful, most patient and most faithful to his friends, for he dedicated a building to his friend Sura, the baths called Suran: he trusted so far in his own innocence that when he gave the praetorian prefect, Suburanus by name, the dagger that was the badge of his power, as the custom was, he often warned him: "I entrust this to you for my protection, if I act rightly; if otherwise, rather against me"; for the ruler of all ought to err even less. He had even moderated by good sense his drinking, a vice from which Nerva too suffered, forbidding orders given after rather long banquets to be carried out. Having ruled with these virtues nearly twenty years, when he was suffering the worst from a severe earthquake at Antioch and the rest of Syria, returning to Italy at the senators' request he died of illness at a great age, having first adopted for the rule Hadrian, his fellow citizen and kinsman. From then on the names of the Caesars and of Augustus were divided, and it was introduced into the state that there should be two or more of supreme power, different in title and unequal in power. Though others think he gained the rule by the favour of Plotina, Trajan's wife, who had pretended that he had been made heir to the throne in her husband's will.

blocks: So Aelius Hadrian, better suited to eloquence and the pursuits of peace, having settled peace in the east, returned to Rome. There, after the manner of the Greeks or of Numa Pompilius, he began to attend to ceremonies, laws, gymnasia and teachers, so much so that he even set up a school of the liberal arts, which they call the Athenaeum, and celebrated at Rome, in the Athenian manner, the mysteries of Ceres and Libera, called the Eleusinian. Then, as usually happens when things are calm, growing more relaxed, he withdrew to his own estate at Tibur, leaving the city to Lucius Aelius Caesar. He himself, as is the way of the fortunate rich, built palaces, attended to banquets, statues and paintings; in short he provided anxiously enough for everything that belonged to luxury and wantonness. From this arose bad rumours that he had debauched youths and burned for Antinous in a notorious service, and that for no other reason had he founded a city in his name or set up statues to the young man. Others, indeed, will have it that these things were pious and religious: for they report that when Hadrian wished to prolong his life, and the magicians had demanded a volunteer to die in his place, when all refused, Antinous offered himself, and hence the honours mentioned above were paid to him. We shall leave the matter open, though in a relaxed character we judge suspect the companionship of men of such unequal age.

Meanwhile, when Aelius Caesar had died, since he himself was weak in mind and for that reason despised, he summoned the senators to make a Caesar. As they hurried to him, he happened to see Antoninus supporting with his hand the anxious steps of his old father-in-law, or his father. Wonderfully pleased at this, he ordered him to be adopted by law as Caesar, and at once ordered a great part of the senate, by whom he had been mocked, to be killed. Not long after he died of a wasting disease at Baiae, in the twenty-second year of his rule less a month, in a still vigorous old age. But the senators could not be moved, even at the emperor's request, to grant him the honour of a god; they so mourned the loss of so many men of their order. But after those whose death they grieved suddenly appeared, and each had embraced his own, they decreed what they had refused.

blocks: And Aurelius Antoninus received the name of Pius. Almost no stain of vice marked him. A man of a very ancient family, from the town of Lanuvium, a senator of the city; so even-tempered and of such good character that he showed plainly that perfect natures are not corrupted by unbroken peace and long ease, and that cities will at last be happy if wisdom rules. blocks: For he took into his family and into the rule Marcus Boionius, who is called Aurelius Antoninus, from the same town, of equal nobility, but far excelling in the study of philosophy and eloquence. Everything he did and planned at home and in war was divine; these things he stained by want of skill in ruling his wife, who had broken out into such wantonness that, staying in Campania, she would sit by the pleasant shores to pick out from the sailors, because they mostly go naked, those fitter for vice.

So when his father-in-law had died at Lorium in the seventy-fifth year of his life, Aurelius at once took his brother Lucius Verus into partnership in power. Under his leadership the Persians, though they had won at first, at last gave way to a triumph, their king being Vologeses. Lucius died within a few days, and hence the material for inventing that he was trapped by his kinsman's treachery; who, they say, since he was tormented by envy of Lucius' deeds, practised a fraud at dinner. For, having smeared one side of a knife with poison, he cut with it a piece of sow's womb, which by design was the only one, and having eaten one part, as is the custom among intimates, he handed the other, which the poison had touched, to his brother. Only minds prone to crime can believe this of so great a man, since it is well enough established that Lucius died of illness at Altinum, a city of Venetia, and that Marcus had so much wisdom, gentleness, innocence and learning that, when he was about to go against the Marcomanni with his son Commodus, whom he had made Caesar, he was surrounded by a crowd of philosophers begging him not to commit himself to an expedition or a battle before he had explained the difficult and hidden points of the schools. So [the text is corrupt here] the uncertainties of war were feared for his safety for the sake of learning; and under his rule the good arts flourished so much that I would count that glory as belonging to the times too. Ambiguities in the laws were wonderfully clarified, and, the formal bail-bond being removed, a convenient rule was introduced for announcing a suit and waiting until the day. Roman citizenship was given to all without distinction, and many cities were founded, colonised, restored and adorned, and above all Carthage of the Carthaginians, which fire had foully consumed, and Ephesus in Asia and Nicomedia in Bithynia, laid low by earthquake, just as in our own time Nicomedia, in the consulship of Cerealis. Triumphs were held over the nations that stretched under king Marcomarus from the city of Pannonia called Carnuntum to the middle of Gaul. So in the eighteenth year of his rule, still vigorous in age, he died at Vindobona, to the greatest grief of all mortals. In short, things granted separately in the case of others, the senators and the people alone decreed for him all together: temples, columns, priests.

blocks: So Septimius, moved by the murder of Pertinax and at the same time by hatred of crimes, with grief and anger, at once dismissed the praetorian cohorts from service, and having killed all of the other party, by decree of the senate enrolled Helvius among the gods; he ordered the name of Salvius and his writings and acts to be abolished; this alone could not be done. So much does the charm of learned arts avail that not even cruel character harms writers in being remembered. Indeed a death of this kind is a glory to the men themselves and a curse on those who do it, since all, and especially later generations, hold that such talents could not have been crushed except by public brigandage and by madness. For this reason all good men, and I more than others, should take heart: born in the country of a poor and unlearned father, I have in these times made my life more honourable by such studies. This I think belongs to our people, which by some fate is sparingly fruitful in good men, yet holds those it has brought forth, each in his own way, as lofty. Like Severus himself, than whom no one was more famous in the state; whom, though he died at an advanced age, they decreed must be mourned with a suspension of business and a eulogy, declaring that it would have been best if that just man had never been born or never died. Clearly because, when they had come back to the innocence of the ancients, as it were to health of mind, they held him too strict in correcting morals but merciful. So virtue, which at the beginning is thought harsh, when it has been attained becomes a pleasure and a delight.

He defeated Pescennius Niger at Cyzicus and Clodius Albinus at Lugdunum and forced them to die; the first of them, holding Egypt as general, had started a war in hope of despotism; the other, the instigator of the killing of Pertinax, when out of fear on that account he was trying to cross to the Britons, a province he had earned from Commodus, had seized the rule in Gaul. Because of their endless slaughter he was thought crueller, and was given the name Pertinax, though many think he took it himself rather, for his like frugality of life: my mind is inclined to believe that it was given him for his harshness. For when a certain man, whom the circumstances of place, as usually happens in civil wars, had brought over to Albinus, after setting out his case, had finally concluded: "What, I ask you, would you do if you were in my place?" he answered: "I would endure what you will." No word or deed was harsher to good men: since the upright blame such dissensions, however zealously begun, on fortune, and allow the right to be bent rather in protecting citizens than in destroying them. But he, eager to wipe out factions, so that he might act more mildly afterwards, preferred to avenge the necessity of the deed, so that men should not gradually, through hope of pardon, go on to public ruin through conspiracies, to which he understood minds were inclined by the fault of the times; and I do not deny that offences which have begun to spread without restraint must be cut out almost more than severely.

He was fortunate and wise, especially in arms, so much so that he never left an engagement except as victor, and he increased the empire by subduing the king of the Persians, named Abgar. No less did he reduce the Arabs, as soon as he attacked them, to subjection in the form of a province. Adiabene too would have passed into the tributaries, had not the poverty of the land been despised. For these great deeds the senators called him by the names Arabicus, Adiabenicus and Parthicus. Undertaking greater things than these, he drove off the enemy and fortified Britain, as far as it was useful, with a wall drawn across the island to the Ocean at either end. Moreover warlike peoples were driven far from Tripolis, in whose town of Lepcis he was born. These deeds, hard to do, were accomplished the more easily because, implacable to offences, he raised every energetic man with rewards. In short he did not let even small brigandage go unpunished, punishing his own men more, because, as a man of experience, he understood that it happened through the fault of the commanders or even through collusion. He was devoted to philosophy, declamation, and in short all liberal studies; and he composed an account of his own life, equal in elegance and truthfulness. He was the author of very fair laws.

From this man, so great at home and abroad, his wife's disgraces took away the height of his glory; he held to her so notoriously that he kept her even when her lust was known and she was accused of conspiracy. That is shameful in the lowest man and in the powerful, and the more so in him, to whom not private persons or individuals or the wicked, but empires and armies, and the vices themselves, gave way. For when, sick in his feet, he was delaying a war and the soldiers bore it anxiously and had made his son Bassianus, who was with him as Caesar, Augustus, he ordered himself to be carried to the tribunal, everyone to be present, and the emperor and the tribunes, centurions and cohorts by whose doing it had happened to be placed there like the accused. When in this fear the victor of so many armies lay on the ground and begged pardon, he said, striking it with his hand: "Do you see that it is the head rather than the feet that rules?" Not long after he died of illness in a town of Britain called Eboracum, in the eighteenth year of his reign. Born moderately low, he was trained first in letters, then in the forum; and when that did not suit him well, as usually happens in straitened circumstances, while trying or seeking various and better things, he climbed to the throne. There, having experienced harder things, toil, cares, fear and altogether everything uncertain, as if a witness of the life of mortals, he said: "I have been everything; nothing is worth it." His funeral, which his sons Geta and Bassianus had brought to Rome, was wonderfully celebrated, and he was laid in the tomb of Marcus, whom he had revered so much that for his sake he persuaded the senate to enrol Commodus among the gods, calling him his brother, and added the name Antoninus to Bassianus, because from Marcus, after many doubtful events, he had taken the beginnings of his offices as advocate of the treasury; for to those who are struggling, the beginnings of good fortune and their authors are remembered.

But his successors, as though they had received war with each other as an order, at once split apart. So Geta, who had his name from his paternal grandfather, since his brother was vexed by his more modest nature, was besieged and died. This victory was made fouler by the death of Papinian, as those curious about history do indeed think; for they say that at that time he had charge of Bassianus' correspondence, and that when he was told, as the custom is, to compose with all speed what was to be sent to Rome, out of grief for Geta he said that parricide was by no means veiled as easily as it was done, and was put to death for it. But this is wickedly absurd, since it is well enough established that he held the praetorian prefecture and that that man could not, without impropriety, have put such an insult on one whom he loved and had taught.

blocks: When they had held supreme power for two years, having fought a battle against the Germans not unsuccessfully, suddenly Antonius Gordianus, proconsul of Africa, was made emperor by the army in his absence at the town of Thysdrus. When he arrived there on being summoned, as though he had been made emperor for that, he was met by a mutiny; when this had been calmed he easily made for Carthage. There, while he was holding a sacrifice in the usual way to avert portents, from fear of which he was not idly troubled, suddenly the victim gave birth. The soothsayers, and he himself most of all (for he was exceedingly skilled in the practice of this science), took it to mean that he was indeed destined to death, but would give birth to rule for his children; and going further in their conjecture they foretold the end of his children too, declaring that they would be gentle and harmless like that beast, yet not long-lived and exposed to plots.

Meanwhile at Rome, when the death of Gordian was learned, at the urging of Domitius the prefect of the city and the other judges were killed indiscriminately by the praetorian cohorts. For Gordian, when he learned that the rule had been offered to him, had sent envoys and letters to Rome holding out rewards in ample measure; and with his murder the soldiers, a kind of men more greedy for money, faithful and good only for gain, were vexed at having been cheated of these. But the senate, fearing that without rulers worse things would happen, as in a captured city, first set up a rotation of powers, then, having enrolled younger men, made Clodius Pupienus and Caecilius Balbinus Caesars.

blocks: And in those same days in Africa the soldiers made Augustus Gordian, the son of Gordian, who happened to be with his father as a member of his staff while still a boy, and then as praetorian prefect; and the nobility did not reject the deed. In short, when he had been summoned, the praetorian forces were destroyed in battle in the unbuilt parts of the city and in the very heart of it by bands of gladiators and an army of recruits. While these things were going on at Rome, the Julii Maximini, whom Thrace happened to be holding at that time, learning what had happened, hurried to Italy. Pupienus finished them off in the siege of Aquileia, after the rest had gradually deserted them when they were beaten in battle. Their rule, by such delays, sought a year more, to two. Not long after, when Clodius and Caecilius had been killed at Rome within the Palace in a tumult of the soldiers, Gordian alone held the throne. And in that year, having enlarged and established the contest of the lustrum which Nero had brought to Rome, he set out against the Persians, having first, in the manner of the ancients, made open the doors of Janus, which Marcus had closed. There, having waged the war with distinction, he perished by the plots of Marcus Philippus, the praetorian prefect, in the sixth year of his rule.

blocks: So Marcus Julius Philippus, an Arab of Trachonitis, having taken his son Philip into partnership, settled affairs in the east, founded the town of Philippopolis in Arabia, and they came to Rome; and having built a lake across the Tiber, because shortage of water troubled that part, they celebrated the thousandth year of the city with games of every kind. And since the name reminds me, in my own time the eleven hundredth year passed, in the consulship of Philip, celebrated with none of the usual solemnities: so small, day by day, is the care for the city of Rome. This, they say, was indeed foretold at that time by prodigies and portents; of which I should like briefly to mention one. For when victims were being sacrificed under the law of the pontiffs, female genitals appeared in the belly of a male pig. The soothsayers interpreted this to portend the weakness of posterity and that vices would prevail. The emperor Philip, thinking this could be thwarted, and also because, passing by, he had happened to see a youth like his son for hire, very honourably decided that the use of male prostitutes must be abolished. Yet it remains: for with the conditions of the place changed it is carried on with worse disgraces, since mortals seek dangerous things more greedily the more they are forbidden. Add to this that the arts of the Etruscans had sung something very different, asserting that while the good for the most part lay low, every softest man would be happy. I think plainly that they did not know the truth. For however prosperous one's success in all things, can anyone be fortunate when shame is lost, while if it is kept the rest is bearable? When this had been done, leaving his son in the city, he himself, though weak in body from age, set out against Decius and fell at Verona, his army routed and lost. When this was learned at Rome, his son was killed in the praetorian camp. They held power for five years.

blocks: But Decius, born in a village of the Sirmians, had climbed by the ranks of military service to the throne, and, the happier for the death of his enemies, he made his son, named Etruscus, Caesar; and at once sending him ahead into Illyricum, he stayed some time at Rome in order to dedicate the walls which he had begun. Meanwhile the head of Jotapianus, who, swelling with his descent from Alexander, had attempted a revolution in Syria and had fallen at the will of the soldiers, was unexpectedly brought to him, as the custom is; and at the same time in those days despotic power was given to Lucius Priscus, who governed the Macedonians as governor, through the onrush of the Goths, after they had plundered most of Thrace and come there. For this reason, when Decius had left Rome as quickly as he could, Julius Valens took the rule, the people being most eager for it. But both were soon killed, the nobility having declared Priscus an enemy of the fatherland. The Decii, pursuing the barbarians across the Danube, fell through the treachery of Brutus, after completing two years of reign. But many report the death of the Decii as glorious; for they say the son fell in the battle line charging too boldly; and the father, when the stricken soldiers said much to console the emperor, said bravely that the loss of one soldier seemed little to him. So, having renewed the war, while he was fighting vigorously he died in the same way.

blocks: So, while they were staying in Rome, Aemilius Aemilianus seized supreme power after corrupting the soldiers. Setting out to crush him, they were killed at Interamna by their own men, in hope of a greater reward from Aemilius, to whom victory came without toil or loss, and at the same time because, being immoderate in luxury and wantonness, they had spoiled the services of goodwill. The senate made his son Gallienus Caesar, and at once the Tiber in full summer overflowed in the manner of a flood. Wise men foretold that the young man's loose character would be ruinous to the state, because he had come summoned from Etruria, from where the river comes. And that indeed came to pass at once. blocks: About the same time Licinius Gallienus, while he was vigorously keeping the Germans away from Gaul, went down in haste into Illyricum. There he defeated at Mursa Ingebus, who, while governing the Pannonians, had been seized by the desire to rule on learning of Valerian's disaster, and soon Regalianus, who, having taken in the soldiers that the disaster at Mursa had left over, had renewed the war. When these things turned out successfully and beyond his hopes, he, as men do, grew slack in prosperity and, together with his son Saloninus, on whom he had conferred the honour of Caesar, gave the Roman state up as if to shipwreck: so that the Goths, passing freely through Thrace, occupied Macedonia and Achaea and the borders of Asia, the Parthians Mesopotamia, brigands or a woman ruled the East, the force of the Alamanni likewise then held Italy, and the tribes of the Franks, having plundered Gaul, held Spain, having laid waste and almost plundered the town of Tarraco, and part, having found ships at the right time, crossed even to Africa; and what Trajan had won beyond the Danube was lost. So, as though winds were raging on all sides, the greatest things were mixed with the smallest and the lowest with the highest over the whole world. And at the same time a plague was raging at Rome, which often arises from heavier cares and despair of mind.

Amid all this he himself went round cookshops and taverns, clung to friendships with pimps and wine-sellers, abandoning himself to his wife Salonina and to a shameful love for the daughter of Attalus, king of the Germans, named Pipa; for which reason civil disturbances too arose, far more terrible. For first of all Postumus, who happened to be commanding against the barbarians in Gaul, had set out to seize the rule; and having driven off a multitude of Germans he was met by the war of Laelianus; having routed him no less successfully, he perished in a tumult of his own men, because he had refused them when they demanded the plunder of the people of Mogontiacum, since they had helped Laelianus. So when he had been killed, Marius, once an ironsmith and not even then very distinguished in military service, took the throne. So everything had fallen to the lowest point, so that rule and the honour of all virtues were a laughing-stock to such men. Hence, indeed, it was said jokingly that it seemed no wonder if Marius was striving to restore the Roman state, which a Marius, founder of the same craft, family and name, had established. When he had been murdered after two days, Victorinus was chosen, equal to Postumus in knowledge of war, but of headlong lust; restraining it at the beginning, after two years of rule, having violated many by force, when he desired the wife of Attitianus and the deed was revealed by her to her husband, the soldiers were secretly inflamed and he was killed in a mutiny at Agrippina. So strong in the army are the factions of the actuarii, among whom Attitianus was counted, that by malice the hardest things are accomplished for those who seek them: a kind of men, especially at this time, worthless, venal, cunning, seditious, greedy for gain, and made as if by nature for committing frauds and hiding them; controlling the supplies, and so hostile to those who care for what is useful and to the fortunes of farmers; wise at the right time in making gifts to those through whose folly and loss they have amassed their wealth. Meanwhile Victoria, having lost her son Victorinus, with the legions approving for a great sum of money, made emperor Tetricus, who, of noble family, was protecting the Aquitanians as governor; and the insignia of Caesar were given to his son Tetricus.

But at Rome Gallienus wickedly persuaded those ignorant of the public misfortune that all was at peace, often, as usually happens when things go as one wishes, holding games and triumphal festivals, so that the pretence would be more readily believed. But after danger was approaching, he at last left the city. For Aureolus, while commanding the legions in Raetia, roused, as is the custom, by the sloth of so idle a leader, took the rule and was marching on Rome. Gallienus routed him in battle at the bridge which is named Aureolus' Bridge after him and forced him into Milan. While he was attacking that city with siege machines of every kind, he perished at the hands of his own men. For Aureolus, when he saw that the hope of raising the siege was empty, cunningly drew up the names of Gallienus' generals and tribunes as though marked out by him for death, and threw the letter from the wall as secretly as he could; and when it was found by chance by those named, it threw into them fear and suspicion that their death had been ordered, but that the letter had slipped out through the carelessness of his servants. For this reason, by the counsel of Aurelian, whose influence and standing in the army were outstanding, they pretended a sally of the enemy, and led him out of his tent in the dead of night, unprotected by guards, as usually happens in a sudden alarm; and he was run through by a spear, whose, in the darkness, is uncertain. So, whether through not knowing who did the killing or because it happened for the public good, the murder went unpunished.

Yet morals have fallen so far that most act out of zeal for themselves rather than for the state, and for power rather than glory. Hence too the force of things and of names has been corrupted, since for the most part the one who is stronger in crime, when he has prevailed by arms, calls those he has crushed, to the public loss, a tyranny removed. Indeed a good many are enrolled among the gods by a like whim who are scarcely worthy of a funeral. If faithful record of deeds did not stand in the way, which neither allows the honourable to be cheated of the rewards of memory nor the wicked to go on to an everlasting and illustrious fame, virtue would be sought in vain, since that true and unique honour would be granted by favour to every worst man and wickedly taken from the good. In short, the senators, compelled by Claudius, because he had taken the rule by Gallienus' choice, called Gallienus a god. For when, from the flow of blood from so serious a wound, he understood that death was upon him, he had sent the insignia of rule to Claudius, who, with the rank of tribune, was holding the garrison force at Ticinum. This was certainly extorted, since neither can the disgraces of Gallienus be hidden while cities exist, and whoever is worst will always be held equal and like to him. So true is it that emperors and the best of mortals go up to heaven, as far as can be guessed, by the honour of their life rather than by titles sought and arranged, or are celebrated as gods only by the fame of men. But the senate, learning of such an end, decreed that his attendants and relations be thrown headlong down the Gemonian steps, and it is well enough established that the advocate of the treasury was brought into the senate house [the text is corrupt here] and hung up with his eyes gouged out, while the crowd, rushing in, with one cry prayed to Mother Earth and the gods below too to give Gallienus a place among the wicked. And had not Claudius, at once, on taking the city of Milan, ordered, as if at the army's demand, that any of them who happened to survive should be spared, the nobility and the people would have raged more fiercely. And the senators, besides the common misfortune of the Roman world, were stung by the insult to their own order, because he was the first, out of fear of his own sloth, lest the rule pass to the best of the nobles, to forbid the senate military service and access to the army. He held power for nine years.

And when the man who seemed to be that one had offered himself, Claudius showed that this service belonged rather to himself, who was in truth the first of the senate and of all. So, with no loss to the army, the barbarians were routed and driven off, after the emperor had given his life as a gift to the state. So much dearer to good men are the safety of the citizens and a long memory of themselves; which serve not only glory but also, by a certain reasoning, the happiness of posterity. Since this Constantius and Constantine and our emperors [a gap in the text] and more welcome to the soldiers through hope of rewards or of licence. And when the man who seemed to be that one had offered himself, Claudius showed that this service belonged rather to himself, who was in truth the first of the senate and of all. So, with no loss to the army, the barbarians were routed and driven off, after the emperor had given his life as a gift to the state. So much dearer to good men are the safety of the citizens and a long memory of themselves; which serve not only glory but also, by a certain reasoning, the happiness of posterity. Since this Constantius and Constantine and our emperors [a gap in the text] and more welcome to the soldiers through hope of rewards or of licence. For this reason the victory was sickly and harsher, since, as is the way of subjects, out of eagerness to sin with impunity they more readily defend slack rule than useful.

blocks: But Aurelian succeeded, and, the more vehement for it, at once, as if remnants of war were left, advanced against the Persians. When they had been destroyed he returned to Italy, whose cities were being afflicted by the harassment of the Alamanni. At the same time, when the Germans had been removed from Gaul, the legions of Tetricus, whom we mentioned above, were cut down, their leader himself betraying them. For Tetricus, when he was often being attacked by the soldiers corrupted through the treachery of the governor Faustinus, had begged Aurelian's protection by letter, and when he arrived, after drawing up his line for show, surrendered himself in the battle. So, as usually happens with no leader, the ranks were thrown into confusion and crushed; he himself, after two years of lofty rule, was led in triumph, and was appointed corrector of Lucania, and his son received pardon and the rank of senator. No less, within the city, the workers of the mint were destroyed, who, at the instigation of Felicissimus the financial officer, had filed down the coinage's mark, and out of fear of punishment had made a war so serious that, engaging on the Caelian hill, they killed about seven thousand fighting men. Having successfully done so many great things, he founded a magnificent temple of the Sun at Rome, adorning it with rich offerings; and so that what had happened under Gallienus should never happen again, he surrounded the city with the strongest walls on a wider circuit; at the same time he provided wisely and generously for the use of pork, so that it should come abundantly to the Roman people; and the fiscal false charges and those of the informers, which had wretchedly afflicted the city, were done away with, the registers and records of such business being burned, and an amnesty decreed after the Greek fashion; besides which, against the custom of soldiers, of whose number he was, he pursued greed, embezzlement and the plunderers of provinces to a monstrous degree. For this reason he was trapped by the crime of a servant to whom he had entrusted the office of secretary, and died at Caenophrurium, since that man, conscious of plunder and of an offence, cunningly composed a document and betrayed it to the tribunes as if out of goodwill, by which they were ordered to be killed; and they, inflamed by that fear, committed the crime.

Meanwhile the soldiers, having lost their emperor, at once sent envoys to Rome, so that the senators might choose an emperor at their own discretion. When they answered that this duty belonged above all to the soldiers themselves, the legions referred it back to them. So on both sides there was a contest of modesty and restraint, a virtue rare in men, especially in matters of this kind, and almost unknown to soldiers. So much could that man do by his severity and his incorruptible ways that the news of his death was ruin to its authors, fear to the wicked, [the text is corrupt here] to the doubtful, longing to every best man, and to no one a cause of insolence or display; and to him alone, as to Romulus, came the semblance of an interregnum, but far more glorious. This deed above all taught that everything turns on itself in the manner of a circle, and that nothing happens which the force of nature cannot bring again in the course of time; further, that by the virtues of emperors affairs are easily raised even when shattered, and that when they are firmer they are thrown headlong by vices.

blocks: So at last, about the sixth month after Aurelian's death, the senate made Tacitus, one of the consulars, emperor, who seemed indeed a gentle one, almost everyone being the happier because the leading men had recovered from the ferocity of the soldiers the right of choosing the emperor. Yet that joy was brief and not of a bearable outcome. For when Tacitus died at Tyana soon after the two hundredth day of his reign, though he had first tortured the authors of Aurelian's murder, and above all the commander Mucapor, because it was by his blow that Aurelian had fallen, Florianus, his brother, had seized the rule with no decision of the senate or the soldiers.

blocks: He, having barely kept hold of the despotism for a month or two, was killed by his own men at Tarsus, after they heard that Probus had been made emperor in Illyricum, a man of vast knowledge of war, and, in training soldiers in various ways and hardening the young, almost a second Hannibal. For as Hannibal planted much of Africa with olives through the legions, whose idleness he thought suspect to the state and to their commanders, in the same way Probus filled Gaul and the Pannonias and the hills of the Moesians with vineyards; this, indeed, after the peoples of the barbarians had been worn down, who had burst in when our emperors were killed by the crime of their own men, and at the same time Saturninus had been killed in the East and Bonosus at Agrippina with his army; for both had attempted despotism, taking up the force which they commanded. For this reason, when everything had been recovered and pacified, he is reported to have said that soon soldiers would be needless. Hence at last, the more provoked, they slaughtered him at Sirmium a little before his sixth year, when they themselves were being forced to drain his native city with channels and a ditch, since it is spoiled by winter waters on its marshy ground.

From then on the power of the soldiers grew strong, and the rule and the right of creating the emperor were snatched from the senate down to our own memory; it is uncertain whether the senate itself wished it out of idleness, or from fear or hatred of dissensions. For military service, lost by the edict of Gallienus, could have been restored when the legions modestly gave way in the reign of Tacitus, and Florianus would not have rashly seized power, nor would the rule be given by the judgement of common soldiers to anyone, however good, while so great and so distinguished an order was in the camp. But while they delight in their ease, and at the same time are fearful for their riches, whose use and abundance they think greater than eternity, they paved the way for soldiers and almost barbarians to rule over themselves and their posterity.

blocks: So Carus, strong in the praetorian prefecture, put on the dress of Augustus, his sons Carinus and Numerianus being Caesars. And since every barbarian people, on learning of the death of Probus, had seized the opportunity to invade, he sent his elder son to protect Gaul and with Numerianus as his companion went straight on into Mesopotamia, because it lies open to the Persians as if to a regular war. There, having routed the enemy, while, too heedlessly greedy for glory, he went beyond Ctesiphon, the famous city of Parthia, he was burned up by a stroke of lightning. Some report that this happened to him justly; for when the oracles had taught that it was permitted to advance in victory as far as the town mentioned, he went further and paid the penalty. So it is hard to turn aside what is fated, and therefore knowledge of the future is superfluous. But Numerianus, having lost his father and thinking the war at the same time finished, while he was leading the army back, was killed by the plots of Aper, the praetorian prefect, his father-in-law. A pain in the young man's eyes offered the opportunity. In short the crime was long concealed, while the corpse was carried shut in a litter as if he were ill, so that his sight should not be hurt by the wind.

blocks: But after the crime was betrayed by the smell of the rotting limbs, by the counsel of the generals and tribunes Valerius Diocletianus, commander of the household troops, was chosen for his wisdom, a great man, yet with these habits: he was the first who, having sought a robe of gold, desired a mass of silk, purple and jewels for his shoes. Though these things are more than befits a citizen, and show a swollen and extravagant mind, they are yet light compared with the rest. For he was the first of all after Caligula and Domitian to allow himself to be called lord in public, and to be worshipped and addressed as a god. From these things, as far as my judgement goes, I have found that all the lowest men, especially when they have reached high places, are immoderate in pride and ambition. Hence Marius in our fathers' memory, hence this man in ours, went beyond the common bearing, since a mind without experience of power is insatiable, like men restored after starvation. So it seems strange to me that most attribute pride to the nobility, which, mindful of its patrician family, has some right to stand out a little as a remedy against the troubles by which it is harassed. But in Valerius these things were covered over by his other good qualities; and by the very fact that he allowed himself to be called lord, he acted as a father; and it is well enough established that the wise man wished to show that the harshness of facts does more harm than that of names.

Meanwhile Carinus, informed of what had happened, hoping that the disturbances breaking out would be the more easily calmed, went quickly to Illyricum by way of Italy. There he routed the army of Julianus and cut him down. For he, while governing the Venetians as corrector, on learning of the death of Carus, eager to seize the rule, had gone out to meet the approaching enemy. But Carinus, when he reached Moesia, at once engaged Diocletian near the Margus, and while he was eagerly pressing the beaten enemy he perished by a blow from his own men, because, unrestrained in lust, he was seducing many soldiers' wives, whose husbands, more hostile, had nevertheless put off their anger and grief until the outcome of the war. When it went more favourably, fearing that a character of this kind would grow more and more insolent with victory, they avenged themselves. This was the end of Carus and his children; Narbo was their homeland, and they ruled two years. So Valerius, at his first assembly before the army, drawing his sword and looking at the sun, swore that he had known nothing of the killing of Numerianus and had not desired the rule, and ran through with a blow Aper, who stood next to him; by whose treachery, as we have shown above, the young man, good and eloquent, and his son-in-law, had died. Pardon was given to the rest, and almost all his enemies were kept, above all a distinguished man named Aristobulus, the praetorian prefect, in their offices. This was new and unheard of within human memory, that in a civil war no one was stripped of fortune, reputation or rank, since we rejoice when it is conducted very dutifully and mildly and a limit is set to exile, proscription and even punishments and killings.

Why should I mention that he took many, even foreigners, into partnership for the sake of protecting or extending Roman rule? For when he learned that after the departure of Carinus, Helianus and Amandus in Gaul, having roused a band of peasants and brigands, whom the inhabitants call Bagaudae, had laid waste the fields far and wide and were attacking many of the cities, he at once ordered Maximian, faithful in friendship, though half a peasant, yet good at war and in ability, to be emperor. Later, from his worship of the deity, the name Herculius was added for him, as Jovius for Valerius; from which name was also given to auxiliary troops far excelling in the army. But Herculius, setting out for Gaul, by routing the enemy or receiving their surrender, had in a short time made everything quiet. In this war Carausius, a citizen of Menapia, stood out for his readier deeds; and for that reason, and also because he was held skilled at steering a ship (in which office he had spent his youth for pay), they put him in charge of preparing a fleet and driving off the Germans who were infesting the seas. Elated by this, since he was crushing many barbarians and not bringing all the plunder to the treasury, out of fear of Herculius, by whom he had learned he had been ordered to be killed, he seized Britain, having grasped the rule. At the same time the Persians were shaking the East severely, and Julianus and the Quinquegentian peoples Africa. Further, at Alexandria in Egypt a man named Achilleus had put on the insignia of despotism. For these reasons they made Julius Constantius and Galerius Maximianus, whose nickname was Armentarius, Caesars, and called them into marriage alliance. The former received the stepdaughter of Herculius, the latter Diocletian's daughter, their earlier marriages being broken off, as Augustus had once done with Tiberius Nero and his daughter Julia. All of these had Illyricum as their homeland: and though they had little culture, being well trained in the hardships of the country and of military service, they were excellent for the state. So it is established that men become upright and wise more readily through a sense of misfortune, and that, on the contrary, those without experience of hardships, since they judge everyone by their own wealth, give less good counsel. But the concord of these men above all showed that natural ability and the practice of good military service, such as they had from the training of Aurelian and Probus, are almost enough for virtue. In short, they looked up to Valerius as a father or in the manner of a great god; how important and how great this is has been shown by the crimes of kinsmen from the founding of the city to our own age.

And since the weight of wars, which we mentioned above, was pressing harder, the rule was divided into four: all the Gauls beyond the Alps were entrusted to Constantius, Africa and Italy to Herculius, the coast of Illyricum as far as the strait of Pontus to Galerius; Valerius kept the rest. From this at last the huge evil of taxes was brought upon part of Italy. For while it all paid the same tax in moderation, so that the army and the emperor, who were always or for the most part present, could be fed, a new law of payments was introduced. This, bearable in the moderation of those times, has grown into ruin in these. Meanwhile, when Jovius set out for Alexandria, the province was entrusted to the Caesar Maximian, so that he should leave the frontiers and advance into Mesopotamia to ward off the attacks of the Persians. Severely harassed by them at first, he at once gathered an army of veterans and recruits and marched against the enemy through Armenia; which is almost the only, or the easier, way of winning. In short, there he brought king Narseus into subjection, and at the same time his children and wives and the royal court. He was so victorious that, had not Valerius, at whose nod everything was done, refused for an uncertain reason, the Roman fasces would have been carried into a new province. Yet a part of the lands more useful to us was won; and since it is being demanded back more fiercely, a new war has lately been undertaken, very serious and destructive. But in Egypt Achilleus was easily driven out and paid the penalty. In Africa things were done in the same way, and to Carausius alone the rule of the island was conceded, after he was thought more suitable to command and to protect the inhabitants against warlike peoples. Six years later, indeed, a man named Allectus trapped him by treachery. Since he was in charge of the treasury by his permission, out of fear of death for his crimes he had extorted the rule by crime. When he had used it briefly, Constantius destroyed him, having sent ahead Asclepiodotus, who commanded the praetorians as prefect, with part of the fleet and the legions. And meanwhile the Marcomanni were cut down, and the whole nation of the Carpi was moved onto our soil, part of which had already been there since Aurelian.

With no less zeal the duties of peace were bound by very fair laws, and the pestilent kind of frumentarii were removed, whom the agentes in rebus of today closely resemble. Though they seemed to have been established to search out and report whether any disturbances arose in the provinces, they made up wicked accusations, spread fear everywhere, especially among all the most remote, and foully plundered everything. At the same time the corn supply of the city and the welfare of the tax-payers were attended to anxiously and carefully, and by the promotion of the more honourable, and on the contrary by the punishment of every wicked man, the pursuit of virtues was increased. The most ancient rites were cared for most purely, and in a wonderful way the heights of Rome and the other cities were adorned with new and beautifully finished walls, above all Carthage, Milan and Nicomedia. Yet while they did these things, they were not free of vices. For Herculius was driven by such lust that he did not restrain the stain of his mind even from the bodies of hostages; Valerius was not honourable enough in his loyalty to his friends, certainly out of fear of discords, since he thought the peace of the partnership could be shaken by disclosures. From this too the strength of the city was, as it were, cut off, the number of the praetorian cohorts and of the people under arms being reduced; for which reason indeed many will have it that he laid down the rule. For, being a searcher into what was coming, when he learned that by fate internal disasters and, as it were, a crash were hanging over the Roman state, after celebrating the twentieth year of his reign, while still in good health he cast off the care of the state, having with the greatest difficulty brought Herculius round to his view, whose power had been a year shorter. And although, with some judging one thing and others another, the truth has been spoiled, to us it seems that by an excellent nature he scorned ambition and came down to the common life.

So it is established that learning, elegance and courtesy are necessary especially for emperors, since without them the gifts of nature are despised as unpolished or even rough, while on the contrary they won eternal glory for Cyrus, king of the Persians.

But in my memory everyone's prayers raised Constantine, though ready in other virtues, to the stars. Had he set a limit to generosity and ambition and to those arts by which, above all, mature minds, advancing too far in eagerness for glory, slip into the opposite, he would not have been far from a god. When he learned that the city and Italy were being laid waste and that armies and two emperors had been driven out or bought off, he settled peace in Gaul and went against Maxentius. At that time among the Carthaginians Alexander, acting as deputy prefect, had stupidly thrown himself on despotism, though he himself was weak with age, more foolish for his peasant and Pannonian parents, and his soldiers, gathered in haste, scarcely had half their arms. In short, Rufius Volusianus the praetorian prefect and military commanders, sent by the tyrant with very few cohorts, finished him off in a slight engagement. Further he was timid and unwarlike and foully prone to idleness, so much so that while war blazed throughout Italy and his men had been routed at Verona, he attended to his usual affairs no less lazily, and was not moved by his father's death. For Herculius, by nature rather violent, and at the same time fearing his son's sloth, had rashly sought the rule again. And when, with tricks arranged under the guise of duty, he harshly tried his son-in-law Constantine, he at last died justly. But Maxentius, more savage day by day, at last advanced with the greatest reluctance from the city to Saxa Rubra, about nine miles, and when, his line cut to pieces, he was fleeing back to Rome, he was caught while crossing the Tiber in the trap which he had laid for the enemy at the Milvian Bridge, in the sixth year of his tyranny. By him too the Circus Maximus was later wonderfully adorned, and a work built for bathing not much different from the others. Statues were set up in the most frequented places, most of them of gold or silver; then a priesthood was decreed in Africa for the Flavian family, and the town of Cirta, which had fallen in the siege of Alexander, was restored and adorned and given the name Constantina. So true is it that nothing is more welcome and more excellent than the expellers of tyrants, whose favour will at last be the greater if they are moderate and restrained. For human minds, cheated of the hope of good, are more bitterly offended when, with a wicked ruler changed, the weight of hardships remains.
