blocks: While these things were going on in Italy, Maximinus in the East, after two years of rule as Augustus, was routed and put to flight by Licinius and died at Tarsus. So power over the Roman world fell to two, who, though they were connected with each other through Flavius' sister, who was married to Licinius, yet because of their different characters could agree only uneasily for three years. For the one had [the text is corrupt here] great other qualities, the other only frugality, and that merely rustic. In short, Constantine protected and received all his enemies, their honours and fortunes remaining, and was so dutiful that he was the first to abolish the old and most horrible punishment of the gibbet and of breaking the legs. Hence he was held a founder, or a god. Licinius set no limit even to tortures in the manner used for slaves, applied to innocent and noble philosophers. When he had been beaten in various battles, since it seemed hard to crush him altogether, and at the same time for the sake of their kinship, the partnership was restored, and their children were taken into the rule as Caesars together, Crispus and Constantine, sons of Flavius, and Licinianus, son of Licinius. That this would scarcely last, nor be happy for those who were taken up, was shown by the daylight darkened by an eclipse of the sun in those same months. And so six years later, the peace being broken, Licinius was beaten in Thrace and withdrew to Chalcedon. There, having taken Martinianus into the rule to help him, he was crushed together with him.

In this way the state began to be run by the will of one man, the children keeping the different names of Caesars: for at that time the badge of Caesar was given to our emperor Constantius. When the elder of them, for an uncertain cause, had died by his father's judgement, suddenly Calocerus, master of the camel herd, madly seized the island of Cyprus under a pretence of kingship. When he had been tortured, as was right, in the manner of slaves or brigands, Constantine turned his great mind to founding a city and shaping religion, and at the same time to renewing the order of the army. And meanwhile the peoples of the Goths and Sarmatians were laid low, and the youngest of all his sons, named Constans, was made Caesar. Wonderful portents showed that through him there would be confusion in the state; for on the night following the day the rule was given, the face of the sky blazed with continuous fire. About two years later he ordered his brother's son, whose name from his father was Dalmatius, to be made Caesar, though the soldiers strongly opposed it. So in the thirty-second year of his rule, having held the whole world for thirteen, aged more than sixty-two, while marching against the Persians, from whom war had begun to break out, he died on an estate very near Nicomedia (they call it Achyrona), when that star which is foul for kingdoms, which they call the long-haired, had foretold it. His body was brought back to the city of his name. This the Roman people bore with the greatest pain, since they thought that by his arms, laws and merciful rule the city of Rome had been, as it were, renewed. A bridge was built over the Danube; camps and forts were placed conveniently in many places. The extraordinary deliveries of oil and corn were abolished, by which Tripolis and Nicaea were bitterly oppressed. The former's ancestors had offered them to their fellow citizen in gratitude for the rule of Severus, and neglect had turned a favour, through the gifts, into ruin for their descendants. The latter Marcus Boionius had punished with a fine, because they had not known that Hipparchus, a man of outstanding genius, was a native of their town. Fiscal oppressions were firmly suppressed, and all would have seemed equal to a divine rite, had he not granted access to public office to men too little worthy. Though this happened rather often, yet in the highest genius and the best character for the state, vices, however small, shine out more and so are easily noticed; indeed they often do more harm, since because of the honour of their author they are taken above all for virtues and are an invitation to imitate them.

So at once Dalmatius was killed, at whose urging is uncertain; and immediately three years later Constantine, the youngest and the eldest, fell in a fatal war. Constans, the more swollen by this victory, and at the same time too little cautious because of his age and violent of mind, further accursed for the wickedness of his ministers and headlong in greed and in contempt of the soldiers, was trapped by the crime of Magnentius in the tenth year after his triumph, though he had certainly suppressed the risings of foreign peoples. It is held for certain that he burned with lust of this kind, because he had kept too elegantly the more handsome boys among their hostages, sought out for a price. Yet would that these vices had remained! For by the cruel and savage character of Magnentius, as being of a barbarian people, and at the same time by what happened afterwards, everything was so destroyed that that rule was not unjustly missed; and also because Vetranio, wholly ignorant of letters and rather stupid in character, and for that reason the worst through his rustic folly, while in command of the infantry in Illyricum, had wickedly seized despotic power, though born in the more squalid parts of Upper Moesia.

The state, lately at rest from civil alarm, had begun to be tried again when Silvanus was forced into the rule. For this Silvanus, born in Gaul of barbarian parents, had earned by his rank in the army, and at the same time by going over from Magnentius to Constantius, the command of the infantry while still rather young. When, from fear or madness, he had climbed higher than that, he was killed in an uproar of the legions, from whom he had hoped for protection, about the twenty-eighth day. For this reason, so that nothing should be changed among the Gauls, who are headlong by nature, especially as the Germans were ravaging most of those parts, he put in charge of the Transalpine lands the Caesar Julian, dear to him through kinship; and he in a short time subdued wild nations, capturing famous kings. Though these things happened through his force, yet they happened by the fortune and counsel of the emperor. This counts for so much that Tiberius and Galerius, while subordinate to others, achieved many outstanding things, but under their own command and auspices achieved fewer of equal worth.

But Julius Constantius, ruling as Augustus for twenty-three years, is kept busy now by foreign, now by civil disturbances, and is scarcely free from arms. Having driven out the tyranny of such great men and meanwhile withstood the attack of the Persians, he took his seat among the people of the Sarmatians with great dignity and gave them a king. We find that Gnaeus Pompeius did this in restoring Tigranes, and scarcely a few of our ancestors. He is calm and merciful as the business requires, wise in the elegance of letters and in a gentle and pleasant kind of speaking; patient of toil and wonderfully quick at aiming arrows; master of all food, lust and all desires; dutiful enough in honouring his father and too watchful of himself; aware that by the life of good emperors the peace of the state is governed. These things, so great and so famous, have been stained by too little care in testing the governors of provinces and of the army, and also by the absurd manners of most of his ministers, and further by the neglect of every good man. And to finish the truth briefly: as nothing is more famous than the emperor himself, so nothing is more savage than most of his attendants.
